segments.say: Most of us have stood in front of someone in pain and felt the same thing: a sense of not knowing what to say. We reach for a sentence that sounds comforting. And often, the sentence lands wrong. Psychologists have studied this, asking both the people who were hurt and the people who tried to help. The gap between the two is one of the most useful findings in the field.

In the 1980s, Camille Wortman and her colleagues began asking bereaved people which responses from others had helped them, and which hadn't. They also asked the friends and relatives who had tried to help what they had tried to say. The two sets of answers did not match.

The researchers interviewed people who had lost a spouse or a child in a car crash. They found that many of the comments that helpers considered comforting, such as advice, attempts to cheer the person up, and statements about the bright side, were rated as unhelpful by the people who received them. Those who helped had often expected their words to be useful. The bereaved had often experienced them as minimising their loss.

show.where: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 1986
show.what: Social support for the bereaved: recipients' and providers' perspectives on what is helpful

segments.say: Each of these has a kind intention. And each, for someone in acute pain, can sound like a way of saying: please feel differently, because your feelings are making me uncomfortable. People rarely mean that. But it's often what is heard.

show.title: Often unhelpful, though well meant
items: Telling them how they should feel
Pointing to the bright side
Saying that time heals
Offering advice about what to do
Telling them about someone who had it worse

segments.say: The same group later described a set of beliefs about loss that many people hold, and that research does not support. They called them myths of coping, and argued that these myths influence how we treat grieving people, and how grieving people treat themselves.

Wortman and Roxane Silver reviewed the literature and challenged several widely held expectations. That distress is inevitable after a loss. That failure to show distress is a sign of a problem. That it's necessary to work through a loss to recover from it. And that recovery always comes, with a return to the way things were. They argued that the evidence showed a much wider variety of reactions than these ideas allowed.

show.where: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 1989
show.what: The myths of coping with loss

segments.say: You may notice that these myths echo what we have seen in this video, such as the stage theory and resilience. They are all variations on one theme: that there's a right way to react, and that anyone who departs from it is at fault. The research says otherwise.

show.title: Four common myths
items: Everyone must go through intense distress
No distress means something is wrong
You have to work through it to recover
You will return to being exactly who you were

segments.say: If those responses so often miss, what works better? The research and the accounts of people who've been there point to a few simple things. They share one feature. They make room for the other person's experience, instead of trying to change it.

Notice how plain they are. None tries to fix, explain or improve. They simply say: I see you, and I'm staying. The line, I don't know what to say, is particularly useful, because it is honest, and it spares both people from pretending. Many grieving people say that it was the most comforting thing anyone told them.

show.title: Responses people often find helpful
items: I'm so sorry, I'm here
Tell me about them, or about what happened
I don't know what to say, but I care
Can I bring dinner on Thursday?
It makes sense that you feel this way

segments.say: It helps to change what we're trying to do. The goal isn't to take the pain away, which we can't do. The goal is to make sure the person isn't alone with it. That's a goal anyone can achieve, even without the right words. Showing up, listening, and returning again are the heart of it.

There's another side. If you are the one who is going through something, you will probably receive some clumsy comments. It can help to know in advance that most come from love, and from the helper's own fear. You're allowed to answer with a simple sentence.

show.title: When you are the one hurting

segments.say: These are not rude. They're tools. People generally want to know what helps, and many are relieved to be told. A friend who hears, just listening is enough, will often feel that a burden has been lifted from them as well.

show.title: Things you may say if you need to
items: Thank you, I know you care
I'd rather not talk about that right now
What would help most is just listening
Could you check on me again next week?

segments.say: You also don't have to show that you're coping well in order to make others feel better. Some people feel an enormous pressure to appear fine. The research suggests that this pressure is common, and that letting it go, with a few safe people at least, is a relief. You're allowed to be as you are.

show.sub: You don't owe anyone a performance

segments.say: Four terms from this chapter. Social support is the help given by others. Minimising is treating someone's pain as smaller than it is. Myths of coping are widely held but unsupported ideas about how people should react. And presence is simply being there. Picture this scene. Two friends visit a man whose wife has died. The first says that at least she is not suffering any more, and that he should try to stay busy. The second says nothing for several minutes, then says that she does not know what to say, but that she has brought soup and will wash the dishes. Later the man cannot recall a word of what the first friend said. He remembers the second sitting with him in the kitchen. The research on what helps would not surprise either of them: presence beats cleverness almost every time.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter
items: Social support
Minimising
Myths of coping
Presence

segments.say: Here's a quick check before you speak to someone who is hurting. Pause and take a breath. Ask yourself whether you're trying to fix the situation, or to be with the person in it. Say what is true, even if it's small, such as, I'm sorry, I'm here. And leave room for silence. Silence can feel awkward to the one who's offering comfort, but to the person in pain, it often feels like permission. They don't need to hurry or to perform. They can simply be, with someone who's willing to sit with them, and that, according to the research, is worth more than almost any sentence we could invent.

show.title: Before you speak to someone who is hurting
items: Pause and breathe
Ask yourself if you are trying to fix or to be with
Say what is true, even if it is small
Leave room for silence

segments.say: A covered dish and two mugs on a kitchen table. No speech, no advice, no explanation. Just the plain message that someone has thought of you. For many people who have been through the worst, it is the small acts like this, and not the clever words, that they remember with gratitude years later.

show.cap: A dish left on the table

segments.say: If you've ever worried that you said the wrong thing to someone in pain, take comfort. The research is clear that being present matters more than being perfect. A clumsy sentence from someone who stays is worth more than a perfect sentence from someone who stays away.

show.sub: You can't say it wrong by caring

segments.say: So what did we learn? That helpers and sufferers often disagree about what helps. That advice and silver linings often miss. That plain presence and practical help work better. And that grief and distress come in more varieties than the myths allow.
In the next chapter, we'll look at the point at which self-help and friends are not enough, and at what professional help can offer.
